citation.title: Deep reinforcement learning for engineering design through topology optimization of elementally discretized design domains
citation.authors: Nathan K. Brown; Anthony P. Garland; Georges M. Fadel; Gang Li

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: For the first tabulated load case at 25% volume fraction, the RL design has 864 J final strain energy versus 964 J for the gradient-based design.
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: No speed-up is claimed; Section 5 says FEA calls make efficiency no key advantage.
claim.alternatives: Abstract and conclusion say RL designs have similar or better compliance performance; Section 5 notes one of six tabulated cases has worse strain energy.

baseline.classical_method: Sigmund 99-line SIMP topology optimization, penalty factor 3, filter radius 1.5 (Section 4.2)
baseline.implementation: 99-line SIMP algorithm (Section 4.2); implementation language for the comparison not stated
baseline.hardware_ml: Intel Core i7-10510U CPU at 1.80 GHz, 16 GB RAM for training (Section 4.1); test hardware not stated
baseline.problem_size: 6 x 6 training; 6 x 6 to 12 x 12 to 24 x 24 progressive test meshes (Sections 4.1-4.2)
baseline.ml_time: not stated; Section 5 reports up to 11, 28 and 144 FEA calls for 6 x 6, 12 x 12 and 24 x 24 design episodes
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated separately; FEAs occur during RL training (Sections 3.2 and 4.1)
baseline.quality_metric: FE-computed final strain energy in J and final volume fraction (Section 4.2, Table 1)
baseline.quality_gap: First Table 1 case: 864 J RL versus 964 J classical at VF 0.25; fourth case: 1853 J RL versus 929 J classical at VF 0.25

R1.evidence: Section 4.2, Table 1: primary outcome compares quality, with no speed comparison.

R2.evidence: Section 4.2, Table 1: primary outcome compares strain energy, not computational speed.

R3.evidence: Section 5: authors expressly say computational efficiency is not a key advantage.

R4.evidence: Section 4.2, Table 1 reports FEA-derived strain energy and volume fractions for six returned designs; Section 5 describes suboptimal cases, but no overall failure or infeasibility rate is given.

notes: Abstract gives a qualitative quality comparison; Table 1 is the first quantitative classical comparison. Section 4.1 names training hardware and time, while Section 5 explicitly discounts computational efficiency. Data Availability points to a public GitHub data directory but does not explicitly identify released runnable code.
